name: DIM supplement

lead: DIM (3,3'-diindolylmethane) is formed when the body digests indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and cabbage, and is sold as a supplement. In acne communities it is used for clearer skin by people with hormonal breakouts.

The idea is that DIM shifts estrogen metabolism and androgen balance, lowering androgen-driven oil. Lab studies report antiestrogenic activity through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and altered sex hormone metabolism. Human research has focused on cancer and other conditions; no clinical studies of DIM for acne were found.

paras: It is taken as a daily oral capsule, often by people whose breakouts follow a hormonal pattern such as along the jawline or around the menstrual cycle. Users generally wait several weeks to a few months before judging skin changes.

Pure DIM carries skin, eye and respiratory irritation hazard labelling. Because it acts on hormone metabolism, people with hormone-sensitive conditions or who take hormonal medication have reason to check with a clinician first. Long-term effects of supplementation for acne have not been studied in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Used off-label for hormonal acne, DIM is taken to shift estrogen and androgen balance, lowering oil and breakouts. The research on DIM concerns hormones and cancer; acne has not been studied.

lead: 3,3'-Diindolylmethane (DIM) is a compound formed when the body digests indole-3-carbinol, which occurs in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage and Brussels sprouts. It is sold as a dietary supplement [1][2].

In looksmaxxing and acne circles, DIM is promoted as an estrogen-metabolism supplement for hormonal acne. The research identified for this article concerns cancer chemoprevention, hormone metabolism and laboratory biology; no clinical studies of DIM for acne or appearance were found.
infobox: Dietary supplement; indole from cruciferous vegetables

paras: Under acidic conditions such as stomach acid, indole-3-carbinol converts to a series of condensation products, of which DIM is a major component, and these are thought to account for many of its biological effects [2].

Glucosinolate breakdown products from cruciferous vegetables are reported to alter the metabolism and activity of sex hormones in ways that could inhibit hormone-sensitive cancers, although epidemiological evidence for an inverse association with cancer risk is mixed [3]. In laboratory work, DIM showed aryl hydrocarbon receptor-mediated antiestrogenic activity [4]. In vitro, DIM has been reported to inhibit histone deacetylases and to bind weakly to cannabinoid receptors [1].
A mouse study examined the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of indole-3-carbinol and its acid condensation products after oral dosing [5].

No studies found for acne or appearance outcomes. Registered human studies of DIM have looked at other conditions, including breast cancer [6][7], prostate cancer [8], thyroid disease [9], lupus [10] and healthy volunteers [11]; several were small, and some were terminated or withdrawn.

The chemical's hazard classification lists skin, eye and respiratory irritation for the pure compound [1]. Long-term safety in people using it for hormonal acne has not been described in studies identified here.
